story.text: Under what conditions does systematisch hergestellte Strukturlosigkeit become a technique of political domination, and how does this concept help us understand the operation of terror in the National Socialist regime and its relation to Hannah Arendt’s theory of totalitarianism?

One further question is whether structural indeterminacy was merely a contingent administrative effect of the Nazi system or a deliberately produced mechanism of rule aimed at undermining stable expectations, legal protection, and normative order.

Totalitarian domination in National Socialism relied on systematisch hergestellte Strukturlosigkeit—a deliberately produced absence of stable legal and administrative structures—which transformed violence into terror by destroying predictable expectations and making individuals utterly dependent on arbitrary power.

This claim holds that Strukturlosigkeit was not accidental “chaos,” but an engineered condition that functionally linked ideology with terror, enabling the regime to replace legal certainty with the Führer’s will and overlapping, competing authorities.

Pohlmann argues that National Socialism created overlapping jurisdictions, contradictory competencies, and perpetual Ausnahmezustände to ensure that individuals could never know which rules applied or which authority prevailed. This manufactured indeterminacy prevented the formation of reliable expectations and made obedience shift from norms to personal power networks.

In his 1990 essay, Pohlmann shows how ideology (racial myth, historical mission) and terror become operationally coupled through Strukturlosigkeit: ideology defines limitless enemies, and structural indeterminacy ensures that repression can strike anyone at any time, transforming Gewalt into Terror by removing procedural predictability.

Popitz’s theory of violence clarifies the mechanism: Gewalt becomes Terror when sanctions are no longer tied to transparent norms or rule-governed procedures. Strukturlosigkeit dissolves these protective structures, producing a space in which arbitrary violence becomes the primary stabilizer of power.

Arendt’s account of totalitarianism in Origins describes a nearly identical dynamic: the destruction of law as a stable frame, the replacement of normative order by the “law of movement,” and the rise of a dual state where formal legality coexists with arbitrary police authority. Strukturlosigkeit provides a sociological formulation of this Arendtian insight.

Arendt’s analysis of Eichmann and the bureaucracy of genocide reinforces this mechanism: the multiplication of agencies, unclear chains of command, and diffusion of responsibility created conditions where “nobody” was responsible and everyone operated within a structurally ambiguous system that enabled mass murder without explicit orders.

Historical studies of the Nazi polycracy confirm that internal competition among agencies (SS, Gestapo, Party Chancellery, ministries) was deliberately fostered. This supports the thesis that Strukturlosigkeit was not a failure of governance but an intentional strategy to prevent institutional autonomy and channel all power toward the Führer.

One challenge is whether the Nazi system was genuinely “structureless” or rather hyper-structured in a different sense: some historians argue that informal norms, personal loyalty networks, and implicit rules created de facto structures that were stable enough to guide action, even if not formally codified.

Another objection is that administrative chaos may have resulted from rapid regime expansion, ideological overreach, and improvisation rather than deliberate planning. If true, Strukturlosigkeit would be an emergent property of an overstrained system, not a consciously engineered technique.

A further competing explanation suggests that terror in National Socialism was driven less by Strukturlosigkeit and more by the radicalization produced by war, competition within the SS, and the logic of cumulative radicalization. In this view, terror escalated despite, not because of, structural indeterminacy.

One boundary condition is that Strukturlosigkeit cannot explain the high degree of logistical coordination in the genocide (transport systems, camp administration). These highly structured operations coexist uneasily with the claim of general structural dissolution and must be integrated into a more nuanced model.
